title: How Que Alicea Built an Environmental Firm in a Male-Dominated Industry
guestBio: Que Alicea is the founder and CEO of Q & A Consulting LLC, an award-winning environmental health and safety firm based in San Francisco specializing in hazardous materials testing, air quality assessments, and compliance for construction and infrastructure projects across California and Nevada. A former medical day spa owner and paramedical aesthetician, she pivoted into industrial hygiene after taking a disaster recovery job — and accidentally built a company in the process. She is a 2026 Enterprising Women of the Year Award recipient, 2025 WRMSDC Supplier of the Year, and 2025 Asian Inc Entrepreneurial Champion of the Year.
excerpt: Que Alicea never set out to run an environmental consulting firm — but a disaster recovery job she took to fund her spa turned into a company she never planned. In this episode, she gets radically honest about self-funding, job-site bias, and why relationships win contracts that certifications can't. This is the permission slip you didn't know you needed.
metaDescription: Que Alicea shares how she accidentally built an award-winning environmental firm in a male-dominated industry — and what it really takes to win.
keyTakeaways: Businesses don't always begin with a polished plan — sometimes the most powerful move is simply walking through the open door in front of you.
Confidence on a job site, a boardroom, or any male-dominated space comes from knowing your material so thoroughly that your expertise speaks before anyone can question your presence.
Overhead doesn't pause for late invoices, so building a financial buffer for the gap between net-30 and net-45 payments isn't optional — it's survival.
Women-owned business certifications like WBENC are a powerful tool for getting on a shorter list, but the relationships you nurture are what actually win the contract.
Every interaction with a client is a deposit into a relationship account — and consistency over time is what earns trust, referrals, and long-term partnerships.
The best businesses are built around a mission that gives you a reason to get up in the morning, not just a revenue target.
Hiring experts in areas outside your zone of genius — rather than trying to master everything yourself — is one of the highest-leverage moves a founder can make.

quiz.title: What Kind of Accidental Entrepreneur Are You?
quiz.description: You don't have to have the perfect plan to build something powerful — but how you move through uncertainty says a lot about your leadership style. Take this quiz to discover your entrepreneurial archetype and find out what your next bold move might look like.

A.name: The Deliberate Pioneer
A.description: You bring structure to spaces that have never had it. Even when you stumbled into your path, you quickly built a framework around it — because operating without one feels like driving without a map. You earn trust by being the most prepared person in the room, and you lead with expertise before you lead with personality. Que's story will remind you that your meticulous approach is a superpower, and that the credibility you've built through deep knowledge is your most unshakeable competitive advantage.

B.name: The Relationship Architect
B.description: For you, every interaction is an investment. You remember birthdays, you send the check-in text, you show up even when there's nothing immediately in it for you — because you know that the contract, the referral, and the open door all trace back to a relationship you nurtured long before the opportunity appeared. Que's philosophy of treating every touch point as a deposit will feel like home to you, and her strategies for turning community into clients will give you a sharper framework for what you're already doing naturally.

C.name: The Resourceful Realist
C.description: You are not waiting for perfect conditions, because you know they don't exist. When the invoice is late and payroll is due, you problem-solve — not panic. You've learned to stretch resources, rent instead of buy, and keep moving even when the runway looks short. Que's unglamorous early-days honesty will hit differently for you, because you recognize that story. This episode will validate everything you've already survived and give you the language to own it with pride.

D.name: The Mission-Led Founder
D.description: You are not in this for the money — and you know it. There's a problem you are compelled to solve, a gap you can't stop seeing, a community you feel called to serve. That mission is what gets you off the floor on the hardest days, and it's also what attracts the right people, clients, and opportunities into your orbit. Que's reflection on building a business that gives you a reason to wake up will resonate at the core of who you are and remind you why you started.

options.text: By becoming the most knowledgeable person in my niche and making that known.
By showing up consistently for people long before I need anything from them.

options.text: Because I saw a way to do something better than what already existed.

content:
What if the business that changed your life wasn't the one you planned? That's exactly what happened to Que Alicea, founder and CEO of Q & A Consulting LLC — and her story might be the most honest conversation about accidental entrepreneurship we've ever had on The Manage Her®.

Que didn't start with a business plan, a bank loan, or a five-year roadmap. She started with a disaster recovery job she took to keep her medical day spa afloat — and somewhere between hazardous materials certifications and construction site walk-throughs, she realized she had built something real. Something that mattered. Something she couldn't walk away from.

The Door She Didn't Know She Was Walking Through

Before environmental consulting, Que was a paramedical aesthetician and medical day spa owner. It sounds like a world away from asbestos abatement and air quality compliance — but as she explains in this episode, the science isn't as different as you'd think. Both fields center on understanding how environmental exposure affects the human body. That intellectual thread connected her past to her future in a way she never could have scripted.

The pivot started practically. She needed income while the spa industry shifted, so she took a disaster recovery contract. That job became an education. That education became a credential. That credential became a contract. And that contract became Q & A Consulting LLC — named not for her initials, but for a philosophy she'd carry into every client relationship: ask questions, then listen.

If you've ever felt like your path has been too winding, too unplanned, or too far from where you thought you'd end up — this is your episode. Que's story is proof that experience compounds in ways you can't always see until you look back.

What It Really Feels Like to Walk Into a Room Where You Don't Look Like Everyone Else

Que doesn't soften this part. She's walked onto job sites where workers turned to her male project manager — before ever acknowledging her. She's sat in rooms where her authority was assumed to belong to someone else. And she's had to make a very deliberate choice about how to respond.

Her answer wasn't to shrink. It was to speak technical. When you know your field cold — when you can drop the vocabulary, cite the standards, and walk the site with the same precision as anyone else in the room — you earn attention in a way that no title on a business card can manufacture. Credibility is a currency, and Que has spent years building her reserves.

But she's also honest about the internal battle. Doubting yourself when the environment around you reflects so little of who you are is not a personal failure — it's a natural response to a system that wasn't designed with you in mind. The work, she says, is learning to trust what you know even when no one in the room is rushing to validate it.

The Unglamorous Truth About Self-Funding a Business

There's a version of the entrepreneurship story that skips the part where you're staring at payroll due on Friday while waiting on a net-45 invoice from a client who paid on time last quarter. Que doesn't skip that part.

The early days of Q & A Consulting were self-funded and scrappy. Lab fees. Rented equipment. The gap between when the work is done and when the money arrives — and the overhead that doesn't care about that gap. She built the business anyway, dollar by dollar, project by project, relationship by relationship.

Landing San Francisco International Airport as a client was the moment the firm felt legitimate. Not because the revenue changed everything overnight, but because it signaled something: you are here, you belong here, and you can compete at this level. Some milestones matter less for what they pay and more for what they prove.

Certification Is a Tool. Relationships Are the Strategy.

Que holds women-owned business certifications — including WBENC — and she's clear about what they do and don't do for you. Certification gets you on a shorter list. It signals legitimacy to procurement teams who are actively seeking diverse suppliers. It opens a door that might otherwise stay closed.

But it doesn't sign the contract. You do.

The relationships Que has built — through the WBEC community, through Sunday check-in texts to clients, through treating every interaction like a deposit in a long-term account — are what actually move business. Certification is the credential. Relationship is the differentiator. If you're investing in one without the other, you're leaving opportunity on the table.

She also talks candidly about the advice that shifted how she thinks about her team: "Hire up." Stop trying to be the expert in everything. Find people who are better than you at the things you're not great at, and let them be great. Your job as a CEO is to build the vision, not to be the bottleneck.

Why She Can't Quit — And Why You Might Not Want To Either

Here's what sits at the center of everything Que shared in this conversation: she didn't build Q & A Consulting for the money. She built it because it gives her a reason to wake up. Because it creates opportunity — for herself, for her team, for the communities her work protects. Because she is solving a real problem, and that problem doesn't disappear just because the work is hard.

If your only reason to start a business is revenue, Que is the first to tell you: the hard days will talk you out of it. But if you're building something that means something — something that pulls you forward even when the invoice is late and the job site is cold and no one in the room is looking at you — that's a foundation that holds.

You don't have to have it all figured out. You just have to take the next step. Que Alicea's story is what happens when you do.
